title: Jeremiah on Trial for His Life
overview: Jeremiah warns that the temple could be destroyed unless the people change, is nearly executed for saying so, and is saved by royal officials, an old precedent and a powerful friend.

parts.label: The warning in the temple (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Early in King Jehoiakim's reign, Jeremiah is told to speak in the temple courtyard, likely at a festival when crowds came from all over Judah, and to leave nothing out. The message has an 'if': turn from wrongdoing and disaster can be called off, but refuse and the temple will end up like Shiloh, an older worship site destroyed long before.

parts.label: Seized and accused (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: Priests, prophets and worshippers grab him and demand his death, repeating his words without the 'if' and treating them as false prophecy, a crime the law punished with death. Royal officials come up from the palace and sit as judges at the New Gate, since trials were usually held at gates.

parts.label: Jeremiah's defense (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Jeremiah takes back nothing: the LORD sent him, and the way out is still open if they change. He puts himself in their hands but warns that killing an innocent messenger would bring guilt on the whole city.

parts.label: The verdict and Micah's example (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: The officials and the crowd now side with Jeremiah, and some elders recall that the prophet Micah foretold Jerusalem's ruin about a century earlier. King Hezekiah did not kill Micah but turned to God, the disaster was held back, and so the elders say killing Jeremiah would be the real danger.

parts.label: The prophet Uriah killed (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: Another prophet, Uriah, gave the same message, fled to Egypt, and was brought back and executed by Jehoiakim, his body dumped in a common burial ground. Scholars are unsure whether this story belongs to the elders' speech or is the writer's own aside showing how real Jeremiah's danger was.

parts.label: Ahikam protects Jeremiah (v. 24)
parts.note: Ahikam, son of King Josiah's royal secretary Shaphan and one of Josiah's own officials, uses his influence to keep Jeremiah from the crowd. Christians have often read this scene alongside Jesus, who was also accused of speaking against the temple and faced a crowd stirred up by leaders.

disagreement: Christians differ on what it means that the LORD would hold back a threatened disaster when people change: some take it as God truly responding and changing course, while others see it as human language for a God whose plans never change.
think: When someone warns you that something you treasure is at risk, what makes it hard to consider that they might be right?
